title: Acquisition: customer value, VIU & A/B testing
source: Session 6 handout (DDM 26/27) – Lilien, Rangaswamy & De Bruyn (2017) ch. 2 & 6, HubSpot on CAC, OMG website case, ESCP chips VIU case
tagline: Acquiring customers costs money – so you must know what customers value and what one customer may cost. This session measures funnel KPIs and CAC, defines customer value (benefits − costs), calculates value-in-use and tests offers with A/B experiments.
goals: calculate **CTR, conversion rate, cost per sale, ROI and CAC**
explain the **customer value equation** and the core/tangible/augmented product
compare **objective, perceptual and behavioural** measures of customer value
calculate **value-in-use (VIU)** – with and without shutdown costs
set up an **A/B test**, explain type I/II errors and pick **t-test vs. chi-square**

blocks.title: Why acquisition matters
items: It generates money to meet costs, pay employees and reinvest in growth
It shows **traction** to investors, partners and influencers
But: acquisition costs rose by **over 50 %** in five years – marketing gets more expensive and customers trust brands less

blocks.title: Acquisition funnel – OMG website version A
blocks.caption: Each stage has its own KPI – check whether the measures of an analytics tool really reflect the stages of the funnel.

blocks.name: Customer acquisition cost
vars: MC = marketing costs of a campaign or period
blocks.note: For an accurate CAC include **all** marketing costs – campaign spend, salaries, events, even materials. CAC makes marketing ROI measurable; the CLV (Session 8) tells you how much you **may** spend.

blocks.title: Startup OMG: which website version performs better?
given: A: 20,000 visitors · 1,298 clicks · 75 sales at 108 € · 1,800 € ad spend
B: 20,000 visitors · 1,056 clicks · 92 sales at 98 € · 2,000 € ad spend
blocks.question: Compute CTR, conversion, cost per sale and ROI.
blocks.result: A wins on clicks, but B is (slightly) better on the bottom line: higher conversion, lower cost per sale, higher ROI.

sections.heading: What is a product?
sections.lead: Anything that can be offered for attention, acquisition, use or consumption and that might satisfy a want or a need – including services (concerts, consulting, an MBA). Is your degree a product?

steps.label: Core product
steps.text: The central need or benefit. “A customer buys a three-inch **hole**, not a three-inch drill bit” (Levitt); “In the factory we make cosmetics; in the store we sell **hope**” (Revlon).

steps.label: Tangible product
steps.text: Features, styling, quality level, brand name and packaging that make the core buyable.

steps.label: Augmented product
steps.text: Additional services and features (delivery, warranty, support) – increasingly important for the overall experience.

blocks.note: A NO at an early gate sends the idea back; a NO late in the life cycle means reposition or harvest.

blocks.title: Example: the launch of Lexus

sides.label: Benefits
points: Engineering, safety, style, fit and finish on European premium level

sides.label: Costs
points: Reduced perceived risk of buying an expensive car

blocks.note: Toyota targeted buyers who wanted a BMW or Mercedes but found them overpriced – high benefits at lower cost made Lexus an outstanding success.

blocks.title: Measures of customer value
head: Family
Method
How it works
rows: Firm's own engineers estimate value: lab tests, alpha tests by employees, simulations – only as good as the firm's understanding of usage
Ask about the effect of **changes** rather than the worth of the whole offer: “If cartridges lasted 20 % longer, what would that be worth to you?”
Maximum willingness to pay for a product given a reference (previous version, main competitor)
5–10 (potential) customers discuss with a moderator for hours – risk of **groupthink**
Respondents state the worth of described concepts
Popular – but everything can be rated “very important”, no trade-offs, no WTP, weak link to behaviour
Rate or choose systematically varied offerings → part-worths (→ S7)
How much more (less) would you pay if a feature were added to (removed from) the benchmark offer?
Infer value from past behaviour, e.g. multinomial logit
Segment purchase databases (American Express) → cross- and up-selling

sections.heading: Value-in-use (VIU)
sections.lead: VIU = the maximum price a customer would pay for the new product so that it costs them exactly as much per year as the reference product. Price below VIU → the customer gains; above → don't buy.

blocks.name: VIU logic – indifference between old and new
blocks.formula: Annual cost_{old} = units_{new} × VIU + other annual costs_{new}
vars: Annual cost_{old} = units × changes per year × price + shutdowns × shutdown cost
blocks.note: The **supplier's margins are distractors** – VIU is about the customer's costs.

blocks.title: ESCP chips (mock exam 2023/24 and 2025/26)
given: 400 chips at 6 €, changed twice per year
New chips last twice as long (changed once per year)
Add-on: maintenance every 12 instead of 6 months; each shutdown costs 1,000 €
blocks.question: VIU without and with shutdown costs? Buy at 14 €?
steps: Without shutdowns: 400 × VIU = 4,800 → VIU = 12 € (one new chip replaces two old ones: 2 × 6 €)
blocks.result: VIU = 12 € (material only) and 14.50 € (incl. shutdowns) → purchase at 14 €. If shutdowns cost 1,200 €, VIU rises to 15 €.

blocks.title: How the VIU of a new chip builds up
Same pattern, 2019/20: Z-rings vs. Y-rings
blocks.text: 250 Z-rings at 8 €, changed every 3 months (4×/year); Y-rings last twice as long → VIU = 16 €. With 3,000 € per shutdown: 8,000 + 12,000 = 500 × VIU + 6,000 → **VIU = 28 €**, so 25 € is a good deal.

items.text: Drawing conclusions about a **population** from a **sample** – for estimation (average satisfaction in my segment?) and hypothesis testing (does the new loyalty programme raise satisfaction?).
**H0** = “no effect”; **H1** = the hypothesised effect. A test decides whether to reject H0 in favour of H1 – and can be wrong.

blocks.title: Test decisions and errors

cells.label: Type I error (α)
cells.text: We believe in an effect that doesn't exist

cells.label: Type II error (β)
cells.text: We miss an effect that exists

blocks.note: A test cannot control both errors at once: fix α (usually **5 %** in social sciences) and use a test that minimises β.

items.text: A marketing experiment that **splits** the audience randomly: version A (control, existing) vs. version B (challenger, one change) – which performs better on a KPI?

sides.label: Design test
points: CTA button blue (A) vs. red (B), same landing page
Result: blue gets more clicks → keep blue

sides.label: User-experience test
points: CTA at the top (A) vs. in the sidebar/bottom (B)
Same share of visitors sees each version

items.label: Higher conversion
items.text: CTA position, colour, anchor text → more leads

items.label: Less cart abandonment
items.text: 40–75 % leave items in the cart – test photos, checkout, shipping display

blocks.title: Sustainable t-shirt: which test for which KPI?
head: KPI
Funnel stage
Data
Test
rows: Metric rating → compare **means** of A and B
blocks.note: The two KPIs can disagree: people may say they would buy the sustainable version but not choose it. Base the launch decision on the KPI closest to the business goal (sales → choice).

blocks.title: When an A/B test fits
blocks.text: One element, two versions, random split, one KPI (“Does the new newsletter design raise CTR?” → yes). Comparing **different products and different customer groups** (“women buying t-shirts vs. men buying shoes”) → not an A/B test. Note the dark side: Google and Facebook run A/B tests on users **without telling them** (Zuboff).

recap: CTR = clicks / visitors; conversion = sales / visitors; cost per sale = spend / sales; ROI = (revenue − spend) / spend; **CAC = MC / CA**.
**Customer value = benefits (functional, psychological, economic) − costs (monetary, risk, inconvenience)**.
Value measures: objective (engineering, indirect questions, VIU), perceptual (unconstrained: focus groups, ratings; constrained: conjoint, benchmarking), behavioural (choice models, data mining).
**VIU**: old annual cost = new units × VIU + remaining costs; price < VIU → buy. Supplier margins are irrelevant.
Type I = reject a true H0 (α = 5 %); type II = keep a false H0 (β).
A/B: one change, random split; means → **t-test**, choice counts → **chi-square**.
exam: VIU mini-case (every recent mock): annual cost, VIU without/with shutdown costs, buy decision, effect of a change in shutdown costs.
KPI calculation of two website versions (CTR, conversion, cost per sale, ROI).
T/F: “Can an A/B test support this decision?”; type I vs. type II error.
traps: Supplier margins (3 €, 8 €) are **distractors** in the VIU case.
Count shutdowns per **year**: every 6 months = 2, every 3 months = 4.
More clicks ≠ better – judge website versions on conversion, cost per sale and ROI.
Not rejecting H0 does not prove H0 – it may be a type II error.
